items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's try to simplify the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\cos{2x}+\sin^2{x}}{\cos{x}}]

Content:
Since the expression contains [MATH: \cos{2x},] we should immediately think of using the double-angle formula for cosine. The question is, which double-angle formula should we use?

Content:
The formula
[MATH: \cos{2x}=\cos^2{x}-\sin^2{x}]
seems like the natural choice because we can see that one of the terms will cancel with the [MATH: \sin^2{x}] term in the numerator. So let's substitute this into our expression and simplify:

Content:
[MATH: (\cos 2x + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x)|= ((\cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x) + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x); = ((\cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x) + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x); = (\cos^{2} x)/(\cos x); = (\cos x ⋅ \cos x)/(\cos x); = (\cos x ⋅ \cos x)/(\cos x); = \cos x]

Content:
So, the expression [MATH: \dfrac{\cos{2x}+\sin^2{x}}{\cos{x}}] is equivalent to [MATH: \cos{x},] and we write
[MATH: \dfrac{\cos{2x}+\sin^2{x}}{\cos{x}} = \cos x.]

Content:
Note: In general, depending on the particular expression we're trying to simplify, we may want to use any one of the following double-angle formulas for cosine:

Content:
[MATH: \cos 2x|= \cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x; \cos 2x|= 2\cos^{2} x − 1; \cos 2x|= 1 − 2\sin^{2} x]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the double-angle formula for cosine: [MATH: \cos{2x}= \cos^2{x}-\sin^2{x}]

Using the double angle formula for cosine, we simplify the given expression, as follows: [MATH: (\cos 2x)/(\cos x + \sin x)|= (\cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x + \sin x); = ((\cos x − \sin x)(\cos x + \sin x))/(\cos x + \sin x); = ((\cos x − \sin x)(\cos x + \sin x))/(\cos x + \sin x); = \cos x − \sin x]

First, we expand the parentheses in the numerator and then simplify, as follows:

[MATH: ((2\cos x − 1)(2\cos x + 1) − 1)/(\sin 2x)|= ((4\cos^{2} x − 1) − 1)/(\sin 2x); = (4\cos^{2} x − 2)/(\sin 2x); = (2(2\cos^{2} x − 1))/(\sin 2x)]

Then, we recall the double-angle formula for cosine: [MATH: \cos{2x} = 2\cos^2{x}-1]

Substituting this into our expression above, we get

[MATH: (2(2\cos^{2} x − 1))/(\sin 2x)|= (2\cos 2x)/(\sin 2x); = 2\cot 2x.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's try to simplify the following expression:

Content:

Content:
The formula

seems like the natural choice because we can see that one of the terms will cancel with the [MATH: \sin^2{x}] term in the numerator. So let's substitute this into our expression and simplify:

Content:
[MATH: (\cos 2x + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x)|= ((\cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x) + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x); = ((\cos^{2} x − \sin^{2} x) + \sin^{2} x)/(\cos x); = (\cos^{2} x)/(\cos x); = (\cos x ⋅ \cos x)/(\cos x); = (\cos x ⋅ \cos x)/(\cos x); = \cos x]

Content:
So, the expression [MATH: \dfrac{\cos{2x}+\sin^2{x}}{\cos{x}}] is equivalent to [MATH: \cos{x},] and we write
[MATH: \dfrac{\cos{2x}+\sin^2{x}}{\cos{x}} = \cos x.]

Note: In general, depending on the particular expression we're trying to simplify, we may want to use any one of the following double-angle formulas for cosine:
